title: I know only the anklets
hookLine: a bundle of jewels, and a brother-in-law who only knows the anklets
carry: touching an elder's feet is honor

lines: FIVE OF US, ON THE MOUNTAIN.
cards: Sugriva has something to show Rama. A while ago, he says, five of us were sitting up here, and we saw a rakshasa flying across the sky carrying a woman. She was crying out: Rama, Lakshmana.
When she saw us below, she dropped her upper cloth and some of her jewelry, tied in a bundle. We kept them safe. He sends someone into the cave to bring them out.

teach.b: Rama sees the cloth and the ornaments and breaks down. He presses them to his chest and weeps. Sita did more than call out.
She left a trail, throwing down what she could to five strangers, hoping someone would get it to Rama. Someone did. Then Rama turns to Lakshmana: do you know these?
Lakshmana's answer isn't what you'd expect. I don't know her armlets, he says. I don't know her earrings.
But I know the anklets, because I bowed at her feet every day.
Through all the years in the forest, Lakshmana kept his eyes lowered before his brother's wife, the way you would before a mother.
And that verse is quoted to explain a gesture you'll see in Hindu homes everywhere: bending to touch the feet of parents, grandparents and teachers, often called pranam or charan sparsh.
The feet are the humblest part of a person. Touching them says: I put my pride below you, and I ask your blessing. Often the elder answers with a hand on your head.
It isn't groveling; it's honor that goes low on purpose. Then the pact becomes real. Rama asks: who took her, and where?
Sugriva admits he doesn't know where Ravana lives, but he promises to find out, and that Rama will have Sita back. A friendship sworn before the fire now has something to hold in its hands.

how: Touching the feet of parents, teachers and elders (pranam or charan sparsh) is a common gesture of respect in many Hindu families, and Lakshmana's words about the anklets are often quoted when it's explained.

o: an armlet worn high on the arm by royal women
an anklet: the jewel Lakshmana knew from bowing
a bundle of cloth dropped from the sky as a sign

games.q: the bundle of jewels — tap the pairs.
p: bending to touch an elder's feet

s: Lakshmana recognizes all of Sita's jewelry
only the anklets, because he bowed at her feet every day.
she threw them down to strangers so they could reach Rama.
he admits he doesn't, and promises to find out.

games.q: at a family gathering, your grandmother walks in. by today's story, what fits?
o: bend to touch her feet, or join your hands, and receive her blessing.
wave from across the room; bowing is just old-fashioned.
games.why: Lakshmana's daily bow is why the anklets were all he knew: honor shown at the feet, every day, watched or not.

practice: Let your gaze drop softly to your own feet. Breathe in and think of someone you honor, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher; breathe out and offer them, silently, the bow Lakshmana gave every day.
If that person is near you this week, you might bend and touch their feet, or simply join your hands. Keep your eyes low and your breath slow.

wordCard.voice: Nupura, an anklet: the one ornament Lakshmana recognizes among Sita's jewels, because he bowed at her feet every day.

orig.note: Sanskrit nūpura: an anklet. the one ornament Lakshmana recognizes.

carryVoice: Your line: touching an elder's feet is honor. Lakshmana knew only the anklets, because he bowed every day. That's day five hundred eighty-four.
